title: Answer every request the terminals send

blocks.text: Your server goes live with a second acquirer, and its terminals' first day goes badly:

items: authorizations time out at the terminal, although your log shows each one approved;
completion advices and reversal repeats arrive again and again;
the acquirer's auditors found track data from your answers in the terminals' logs;
and your own transaction log records responses where the requests should be.

blocks.text: The terminals' client runs a QMUX with its key set to `41, 11, 37`. The acquirer's specification lists the data elements it wants back in every response; they are `RETURNED` in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/Responder.java`.

Finish the two methods marked `TODO` in that file: `turnAround`, which starts the answer to any request the terminals send, and `addApproval`. `answer` already puts them together. About six lines in total.
The tests send each request through a real QMUX and the 1987 ASCII packager, both ways, and look at what the terminal's client receives and at the request your code was handed.

cases.says: an approved purchase reaches the terminal's client as its answer, with the approval code
a declined purchase reaches the terminal's client as its answer, with the response code
a completion advice gets an answer its client recognises, so it is not sent again
the repeat of a reversal gets an answer its client recognises, so it is not repeated again
a client that also matches on the retrieval reference number recognises the answer
expiry, track data, PIN block and chip data never go back to the terminal
the request the server was handed is still the request after it has been answered
a declined request carries no approval code

origin.section: 2.5 A Response Copies What Identifies the Request, and Leaves the Request Alone

concepts: The client finds an answer by its key fields, so a response must carry each of them unchanged; a response built from scratch or renumbered by the server matches nothing.
setResponseMTI turns any request into its response MTI, while a hand-written MTI leaves other kinds of request, such as advices, unanswered.
A response is a new message holding only the listed fields, so card secrets stay behind and the request in the Context stays a request; the approval code goes only with an approval.
